prompt.raw:
[{"content":"You are extracting a teacher's spoken notes about the children in one class.

The notes arrive as a transcript, in the order the teacher spoke them. The children in this
class are listed below. Names in the transcript are speech-to-text and often misspelt or
mangled; match a spoken name to the listed child it most plausibly is.

Return "observations": the transcript cut into contiguous passages, in order, one passage
per owner, together covering the whole transcript.

Each passage has:
- "kind":
  - "child" — the teacher is talking about one individual child and speaks a name for them.
  - "unknown" — the teacher is talking about one individual child but no name is spoken for
    them in this passage or the passage it continues: only a pronoun, or a name that
    matches nobody listed. Do not guess. The teacher will assign it.
  - "group" — a statement about the class as a whole, using a collective referent
    ("everyone", "all the kids", "the class", "they" meaning the whole group). A statement
    that names one child, or describes only one child, is NEVER "group", however it is
    joined to the rest of the sentence.
  - "none" — not an observation about children: the date, the class header, a greeting,
    vocabulary the children are being taught, thinking aloud that describes no child and
    no class.
- "spoken_labels": for a "child" passage, the name the teacher speaks for it, verbatim as
  spoken, uncorrected. Empty list for "unknown", "group" and "none".
- "student": for a "child" passage, the listed child's name exactly as listed below, or ""
  when no listed child fits. "" for every other kind.
- "summary": the observations in that passage, rewritten as clear sentences.

Rules:
- A child passage runs from where the teacher starts talking about that child to where the
  teacher moves on. It usually opens with the child's name and then continues in pronouns;
  every pronoun sentence after that name belongs to that child until the next child is
  named. Do NOT open a new passage for a pronoun the teacher is still using for the same
  child.
- When the teacher makes the same observation about several named children at once
  ("Zachariah and Anaya did very well", "they both worked well"), return that passage once
  PER CHILD: the same summary repeated, each copy with its own "student". Never fold two
  named children into one passage. If the observations differ between the children, they
  are separate passages with different summaries. A statement about the class as a whole
  is still one "group" passage, not one per child.
- "student" is set ONLY when the passage's own words, or the passage it continues, speak
  a name for the child — a name that appears in "spoken_labels". A passage that refers to
  the child only by a pronoun ("she", "he") has NO student: it is "unknown", even when
  exactly one listed child has not been mentioned yet. Children on the list who are never
  named were absent or not discussed today. Never assign a passage to a child by
  elimination, by roster order, or because they are the only one left.
- The list of children exists to spell spoken names correctly, not to decide who is
  present.
- The summary uses ONLY the words in its own passage. Never bring in an observation from
  another passage, even an adjacent one.
- The summary keeps the teacher's voice: their vocabulary, their tone, first person if they
  used it. Clean up false starts, filler words and repetitions. Do NOT soften, formalise,
  add or editorialise.
- "none" never takes an observation with it. The header passage ends with the header
  itself: the first sentence that describes the children opens a new passage, even when it
  is spoken in the same breath.

The children in this class:
- Emma
- Ryan
- Lila
","role":"system"},{"content":"Class A, Tuesday afternoon. Um, so today I wanted to talk about Emma. She, uh, she did great in math today, really got the hang of the multiplication tables we've been working on. And then, let's see... I also wanted to mention Ryan. Ryan was, he was really struggling with the reading comprehension exercise, couldn't quite get the main idea from the passage. Yeah, that's, that's about it for today.","role":"user"}]

    matches nobody listed. Do not guess. The teacher will assign it.
  - "group" — a statement about the class as a whole, using a collective referent
    ("everyone", "all the kids", "the class", "they" meaning the whole group). A statement
    that names one child, or describes only one child, is NEVER "group", however it is
    joined to the rest of the sentence.
  - "none" — not an observation about children: the date, the class header, a greeting,
    vocabulary the children are being taught, thinking aloud that describes no child and
    no class.
- "spoken_labels": for a "child" passage, the name the teacher speaks for it, verbatim as
  spoken, uncorrected. Empty list for "unknown", "group" and "none".
- "student": for a "child" passage, the listed child's name exactly as listed below, or ""
  when no listed child fits. "" for every other kind.
- "summary": the observations in that passage, rewritten as clear sentences.

Rules:
- A child passage runs from where the teacher starts talking about that child to where the
  teacher moves on. It usually opens with the child's name and then continues in pronouns;
  every pronoun sentence after that name belongs to that child until the next child is

  child.

  PER CHILD: the same summary repeated, each copy with its own "student". Never fold two

  are separate passages with different summaries. A statement about the class as a whole
  is still one "group" passage, not one per child.

  exactly one listed child has not been mentioned yet. Children on the list who are never
  named were absent or not discussed today. Never assign a passage to a child by
  elimination, by roster order, or because they are the only one left.

  another passage, even an adjacent one.

  used it. Clean up false starts, filler words and repetitions. Do NOT soften, formalise,
  add or editorialise.

  itself: the first sentence that describes the children opens a new passage, even when it

- Séverin

Objectives and content of the Oliver course, 3rd term

---

Term report (3rd term)

Data

  • Name: Mila
  • Teacher: Thérèse Garnier
  • Level: Oliver · Thu 2025/2026
  • Period: 2026-02-22 to 2026-05-22

Participation/Motivation

Assessment (Participation / Motivation): Good

Comment: Mila generally comes to class in a positive mood and shows interest in the activities presented. She is usually willing to participate and can be very engaged when she feels comfortable with the task, especially in action-based activities and games. At times, however, she can become upset when things do not go as she expects, which affects her willingness to continue taking part. With encouragement, she is able to rejoin the class and show good motivation, particularly when she has the opportunity to help or demonstrate what she knows.

Learning process

Assessment (Learning process): Good

Comment: Mila has shown good understanding of the structures and vocabulary worked on this term. She can repeat the target language well and, in many activities, uses the new language with confidence. Her knowledge of the story has improved notably, and she is able to retell parts of it with little support. She also performs very well in activities involving weather, clothing, and colour vocabulary. At times, she still needs help with some specific words and routines, such as taking off and putting on, and she may need further practice to remain consistent when new language is introduced. Continued repetition and reinforcement will help her consolidate her progress even further.

Behaviour

Assessment (Behaviour): Good

Comment: Mila is well integrated in the group and can participate positively in class. On the whole, she behaves appropriately and works well with the rest of the students, especially during practical and familiar activities. However, when she becomes frustrated or does not get her way, she may withdraw, refuse to participate, or show signs of anger, which can affect her focus during the lesson. She sometimes needs reminders to stay engaged and remain seated during story time. When she is calm, she responds well and shows a much more cooperative attitude.

Marks

Oral Test Mark: 8.00    Good. Mila can understand the question and answers either with a single word or with a structure which is only partially correct.

Final comment

Mila has made good progress this term and has shown that she can understand and use a great deal of the language worked on in class. Her ability to repeat structures, recognise vocabulary, and take part in action activities is very promising. With continued encouragement to manage moments of frustration and to stay engaged throughout the whole lesson, she will be able to keep building confidence and continue developing her English skills successfully.

MOTIVATION AND PARTICIPATION

Mila demonstrates a generally positive attitude towards classroom activities, arriving in a happy mood and showing willingness to engage with new tasks. She is cooperative with the teacher and her peers, though she occasionally closes up when things do not go her way. For example, she initially struggled with the "taking off" and "putting on" vocabulary during weather routines but persisted with support. Mila is open to participating in new activities, such as combining moods with actions or using new vocabulary like colors ("white" and "black").

Her participation varies depending on the activity. Mila is highly engaged when she can apply previously acquired knowledge, such as telling the story with minimal help or combining weather cards with actions. However, she sometimes holds back when faced with challenges, like when she refused to participate in the True or False activity and Dice Game after not being allowed to keep the blu-tack. She also showed reluctance at times, such as when she laid down during story time due to frustration over not seeing the Big Book, though she eventually complied when asked to sit.

BEHAVIOUR

Mila is generally well-integrated within the group, though her behaviour can be influenced by her mood or specific frustrations. For instance, she turned her back during story time when upset but did not disrupt the class. Her reactions to situations, such as not getting her way or being denied a small item, sometimes led to temporary withdrawal, though she typically re-engages with support. The group’s energy levels, such as restlessness towards the end of the story, did not significantly impact her focus once she refocused.

LEARNING

Mila has shown strong progress in using structures and vocabulary from the lessons. She could repeat and apply familiar structures well, such as weather routines and clothing items, though she needed occasional help with specific phrases like "taking off" and "putting on." Her ability to combine moods with actions and use new vocabulary (e.g., colors) demonstrates a solid grasp of the material. She also excelled in activities like the worksheet on weather and clothing combinations.

Strengths: Mila’s confidence in storytelling and her ability to recall and use structures and vocabulary are notable. She actively participates in action-based activities and shows enthusiasm for tasks like "A present for me" and "Family Bingo."

Weaknesses and Improvement Plan: Mila occasionally struggles with frustration when things do not go as planned, which can temporarily affect her participation. To support her, the school will encourage her to express her feelings constructively and provide gentle reminders to stay engaged during challenging moments. We will continue to build her resilience by praising her efforts and progress, even when tasks are difficult.

MOTIVATION AND PARTICIPATION

Mila demonstrates a positive attitude when entering the classroom, often appearing in a happy mood. She shows willingness to learn and actively participates in classroom activities, including story time, action activities, and group games such as "A present for me," "Family Bingo," and the "Dice Game."

Mila is generally open to new activities and demonstrates enthusiasm when tasks align with her understanding. However, she can become upset when expectations are not met, such as when she could not see the Big Book during story time or when she was not allowed to keep the blu-tack. These moments of frustration occasionally lead her to hold back or refuse participation in certain activities, such as the True or False activity and the Dice Game.

Her participation is particularly strong in activities she enjoys or finds manageable, such as combining moods with actions, using weather cards, and completing worksheet activities. She shows a competitive spirit and strives to do well, which motivates her to engage actively when she feels confident.

BEHAVIOUR

Mila is generally well-integrated within the group and participates in class activities alongside her peers. However, she can become easily distracted or upset during activities that do not meet her expectations, such as story time when she could not see the Big Book. On these occasions, she may lay down or turn her back to the teacher, indicating her frustration.

The overall mood of the group can influence her behaviour, as seen when the class seemed to get bored by the end of the story. Additionally, Mila’s mood can vary; she was notably happy on some days but upset on others, such as when she mentioned having a headache but still participated in activities.

In situations that required specific plans, such as managing her frustration during activities, Mila initially struggled but showed improvement over time. For example, she closed up when she did not get her way but eventually participated more actively.

LEARNING

Strengths:

  • Mila has a strong grasp of the vocabulary and structures worked on during the story, including songs, gestures, and phrases related to weather and clothing items.
  • She can combine moods with actions effectively and use phrases correctly with her weather cards.
  • Mila demonstrates a good understanding of the story, being able to tell part of it and repeat the rest with minimal help.
  • She performs exceptionally well in worksheet activities and color vocabulary tasks, showing confidence in her knowledge.

Areas for Improvement and School Commitment:

  • Mila sometimes struggles with new or challenging tasks, such as the "taking off" and "putting on" words during weather routines, which can lead to frustration. The school will work on providing additional support and encouragement during these activities to help her build confidence.
  • Her willingness to participate can waver when she is upset or feels that she is not succeeding, as seen when she refused to take part in the True or False activity and the Dice Game. The school will implement strategies to help her manage her emotions and foster a more positive attitude towards challenges.
  • Mila may hold back when new material is introduced, but she participates more actively once the material is internalized. The school will ensure that new concepts are reinforced through engaging and supportive activities to encourage her participation from the start.

```html

MOTIVATION AND PARTICIPATION

Motivation

Camille demonstrates a positive attitude towards classroom activities, showing attentiveness and engagement throughout the lessons. She displays willingness to learn by participating actively in activities and demonstrating understanding of the material presented. Camille is open to new activities, particularly enjoying interactive games such as "A present for me," Family Bingo, and the Dice Game. She cooperates with both the teacher and peers, though occasional moments of distraction with classmates are noted.

Participation

Camille participates enthusiastically in activities she finds engaging, such as storytelling, vocabulary recall, and interactive games. She shows a strong desire to be involved, often volunteering for tasks and demonstrating competitiveness in group activities. Her participation is particularly notable when new routines or games are introduced, as she quickly adapts and contributes. However, she occasionally requires reminders to use correct structures during activities and may hold back slightly when new material is introduced, though she warms up as the activity progresses.

BEHAVIOUR

Camille is generally well-integrated within her group, interacting positively with peers such as Zoé during activities. While she occasionally becomes distracted while playing with classmates, her overall behaviour remains appropriate and she refocuses well. Her mood and energy levels appear to fluctuate slightly, with moments of hesitation noted during new routines, but encouragement from the teacher helps her regain confidence. The classroom environment and group dynamics do not appear to negatively impact her behaviour, as she remains engaged and cooperative throughout most activities.

LEARNING

Camille demonstrates solid progress in her learning objectives. She shows strong memorisation of vocabulary, particularly colors, clothing items, and prepositions, and can recall parts of the story with prompting. Her understanding of worksheet activities is evident, though she occasionally needs reminders to use correct structures. She quickly grasps new routines, such as weather and action miming, as well as mood expressions (e.g., "he's smiling because he's happy").

Strengths

  • Quick adaptation to new routines and activities
  • Active participation in games and interactive tasks
  • Positive attitude towards learning and trying new activities

Weaknesses and Improvement Plan

  • Area for improvement: Continued practice in asking questions about a person's physical appearance before identifying them remains a work in progress.
  • School's commitment: The teacher will provide additional structure reminders during activities and encourage Camille to formulate questions more independently to strengthen her participation in discussions.
